title: Cultivation No-Dig
stage: Three-photo greenhouse-facing page proof for review
site: The no-dig bed at the porch end of the back garden. Camera faces the greenhouses. A small strip of grass on the right is an imagined addition requested by John.
timing: Day one: distribute surface compost using a garden fork
One week later: begin planting lettuce
wardrobe: Teal fleece, olive beanie and jeans
J01 checked shirt with blue jeans, bareheaded

joint_render.prompt:
Make a matched photographic triptych for John Lennon's UK vegetable gardening book. Three separate SQUARE photographs in one continuous 3:1 horizontal canvas, about 2172x724 or larger. Simple hard joins at thirds, no gaps, graphics, titles, numbers, arrows or text. Each is a full-bleed photograph, judged at 45mm square in print. EXACT location, greenhouse-facing camera angle and man from reference 1, already approved by the owner. Same bed and same perspective across the sequence, with an extra strip of grass requested beyond the bed on the right. Reference 2 is an authentic image of the same bed from the same side; its far landforms and greenhouse structure are a check only. Reference 3 is the real actor looking down with his characteristically receding chin; ref 4 gives the actual checked shirt, hair and face for panel three.

In all THREE: Camera at the porch end facing AWAY from house towards the greenhouses. No porch, old planter at far right, windows of a house, building or water butt on the near right anywhere in the scene. Keep the pale aluminium greenhouse on its low masonry plinth across the upper left with its long glazed wall receding towards the wooden rear fence, large berry planter and part of the blue shed at far left, modest transverse low raised bed at the far end as reference 1. Register the same far bed corner to the same greenhouse post, and the camera distance to the kneeling John. Let the eye follow the same bed from broad near end to narrower far end. Widen the real bed so it is visibly 1.2 metres (four feet) ACROSS, 4–5 metres long. A broad reachable 1.2 m working bed, not a narrow strip. In perspective its near short edge should be two to three times the width of John's shoulders WHEN MEASURED AT HIS SAME DEPTH. For scale, slightly more than four adult work boot lengths ACROSS it. Show BOTH front corners, clearly and wholly inside each square, and a continuous little 25–40 cm margin of short, true-green lawn BEYOND the right long edge, from front to back. Achieve this by stepping the camera back slightly from the approved frame, retain direction, no forehead chop or tiny distant people. The foreground composition uses available width for John on the grass at left, the FULL broad bed in the middle, and a narrow band of grass along the right edge. Broad edge distinction at the printed size. No high wooden/frame sides. Short freshly cut domestic grass showing subtle natural wear. Permanent greenhouse and bed footprint absolutely steady in all frames. Natural Cornish spring daylight. Keep face and hands legible, tools physically coherent. John's receding chin sits well behind lower lip, short greying beard follows the jaw and retreats into collar when looking down (ref 3).

LEFT — covering the intact turf: reproduce the approved pose/teal fleece/olive knit cap/jeans. John kneels on grass to the LEFT of the broad bed, leaning right, overlaps damp, plain flattened brown corrugated cardboard cartons directly on the cut grass. Two offset runs of large overlapping cartons ACROSS the width and repeated away from us; convincing uneven folds, different shades. Near sheet's edge raised a little in his fingers to show a generous overlap, with a little grass around its edge. No printing, labels or tape, no compost. 
CENTRE — spreading compost on the same day: still teal fleece, olive cap and jeans, John stands relaxed on the left grass in the same foreground working zone. His ONLY implement is a commonplace UK FOUR-TINED GARDEN FORK, single centred wooden shaft, D handle, one forged neck and FOUR conventional thick, forward-curving steel prongs pointing in the same direction as the shaft. Tool head about handspan width, similar in shape to a big dinner fork, never the wide transverse head of a rake. John is caught MID-SPREAD as he eases a small forkful of well-rotted, crumbly compost sideways off the tines onto a slightly lower part of the surface, with fork held shallowly, no tines plunging into the underlying grass/cardboard. One hand on D-grip, one lower on shaft. Dark mature compost about 10 cm deep across the broad bed with a few irregular low heaps being levelled, last bit of cardboard showing at unfinished far end. No digging or turning soil; this is the compost-spreading action. No rake anywhere.
RIGHT — literally the beginning of planting a week later: slightly lighter spring daylight and same bed and lawn. John kneels on LEFT grass bare-headed, checked cream and charcoal overshirt over dark T-shirt, rolled sleeves, blue jeans, look like ref 4. Place a real compact BLACK PLASTIC MODULE TRAY of little green lettuce seedlings ON THE GRASS immediately beside his knee, clear of the bed. Mostly full grid of plugs with two or three empty cells. Let tray be easily recognised in its own clean area down left, not tucked behind him. EXACTLY TWO small lettuces ALREADY in the compost, BOTH near the working end, about 30 cm apart and plenty of room around them. John lifting one further plug, its little dark rootball clearly ABOVE the compost, about to set it in. The rest of the long, broad bed behind those two plants is clearly EMPTY, uninterrupted dark level compost to the far end; no seedlings dotted along it, no decorative row. No trowel needed, relaxed hands. Plastic nursery tray stays on the grass, no pot clutter. Same strong face likeness as approved, ordinary documentary photo. Bare beds in foreground separate from established greenery behind. 
Across all three squares make right grass verge clear and bed width steady and convincing. The setting, actor, materials and scale must feel like a real visit and a return visit to the same Cornish garden.
